absent: Traversal order, address selection, and error conditions of architecture stack walk helpers.
Numeric values of overflow defaults, niceness bounds, priority classes, and signal or error codes.
Semantics of task stack pinning, register access, scheduler function test, and completion waiting.
Capability, security hook, and user reference lifetime rules for priority changes.
Memory ordering and acquisition rules for per CPU access, RCU, task list lock, atomics, and interrupt control.
CPU hotplug, scheduler stop class binding, and per CPU thread registration effects.
Sysctl registration, naming, modes, and handler enforcement for overflow identifiers.

findings.text: Provides a formatter that renders an array of captured addresses into a caller supplied character buffer with leading spacing and symbolic decoding, advancing through available space and reporting the total length that would have been produced even when truncated.
Formatter treats a missing address array as a programmer error, emitting a warning and producing no output rather than dereferencing it.
Collector for stack walk results pairing a destination array and its capacity with a count of initial addresses to discard and a count of addresses already retained.
Bounded collector first satisfies any outstanding skip quota, then stores the address only while capacity remains, and reports whether further collection can continue.
Scheduling aware collector variant silently ignores addresses that belong to scheduler functions and otherwise behaves like the bounded collector.
Captures a register anchored kernel stack for the running task into a caller array, honouring a caller supplied skip count and returning how many addresses were stored.

Reliable per task capture treats a task without an accessible stack, such as a zombie, as reliably empty with zero entries, otherwise pins the stack during the walk, releases it afterwards, and returns either a walk error or the stored count.
User stack capture returns no entries for kernel threads and otherwise walks the user stack of the current task using its saved registers.

Alternate capture entry points adapt a legacy trace descriptor carrying destination, capacity and skip to older walk helpers and return the resulting entry count; the register based legacy helper is unimplemented and only warns once.
Interrupt stack filtering detects membership in hard interrupt entry and soft interrupt entry address intervals and truncates an address list just after the first such entry, keeping that entry.
Completion tracker for coordinated CPU stops combining a remaining worker count, a collected return status, and a completion signal raised when the count reaches zero.

Per CPU stopper state combining a dedicated thread, a raw spin lock, an enabled flag, a queue of pending requests, a preallocated request for coordinated stops, plus recorded caller and callback for diagnostics.
Stopper diagnostic helper produces output only when the examined task is the stopper thread of its CPU, identifying the active callback and its caller.
Global stop coordination is serialized by a mutex with a companion progress flag that lets contended two CPU queueing detect a race, back off, wait for clearance, and retry.

Synchronous single CPU execution queues one callback with caller identity, yields if targeting the local CPU to avoid sleep wakeup overhead, waits for completion, and reports either queue absence or the callback status.

Coordinated stop progresses through idle, preparation, interrupt disabling, execution, and exit phases, with participants acknowledging each phase and the final acknowledger advancing the shared state.
Coordinated stop descriptor carries the callback and its argument, the expected participant count, an optional active subset mask, the current phase, and an outstanding acknowledgment count.

Worker for coordinated stops selects an active set defaulting to all online CPUs, preserves interrupt flag state, spins yielding until the phase changes, disables interrupts in the disable phase, runs the callback only on active members in the run phase, suppresses lockup and stall reports while waiting past preparation, acknowledges each new phase, and restores flags before returning its status.

Two CPU queueing disables preemption, acquires both stopper locks in ascending CPU order with nesting, validates that both stoppers are enabled, refuses to interleave with an in progress multi CPU queue, enqueues both requests atomically, releases locks, retries after backoff on contention, and wakes both threads only on success.

Synchronous paired execution runs the same callback on two CPUs via the coordinated worker, ordering the CPU identifiers to respect lock order, initializing completion for two participants, and waiting before returning the collected status or queue absence.
Asynchronous single CPU request fills a caller supplied work buffer with callback, argument and caller identity and queues it without waiting, warning if the target stopper is unavailable.
Stopper run predicate and draining thread guard the pending queue with the per CPU raw spin lock held with interrupts disabled, testing emptiness and unlinking the first entry under that lock.

Stopper thread executes queued callbacks with preemption counting elevated to forbid sleeping, records caller and callback for diagnostics, folds any nonzero return into the shared status, signals completion, clears diagnostic fields, warns on leaked preemption count, and repeats until the queue is empty.
Stop callbacks execute in atomic context and must not sleep; parking warns if any work remains queued, indicating a lifecycle violation.

Stopper threads are modelled as self parking per CPU hotplug threads with a defined run predicate, thread body, creation hook binding the thread to the scheduler stop class, park hook, and migration style naming; early initialization prepares each lock and queue, registers the threads, unparks the boot CPU, and marks the facility ready.
Global stop prevents CPU arrival or departure for its duration, then delegates to a locked variant that runs the callback across the requested CPUs.
Core scoped stop requires the CPU hotplug lock to be held, targets the sibling mask of the given CPU with a matching participant count, and runs the callback through the coordinated worker.

Stop issued from an inactive CPU requires the local CPU to be inactive during hotplug, counts active CPUs plus local, busy waits for the global mutex without sleeping, queues work to active CPUs, runs the local participant directly, busy waits for remote completion, and combines local and remote statuses.

Architecture specific process control fallbacks for alignment, floating point emulation and exception, endian, timestamp counter, floating point mode, vector lengths, pointer authentication, tagged addresses, RISC-V vector and icache, and PowerPC DEXCR aspects uniformly report invalid argument when the architecture provides no implementation.

Fixed overflow identifiers for user, group and filesystem user and group exist with compile time defaults and the user and group variants are exposed as writable kernel sysctl entries constrained to a numeric range.
Priority change permission is granted when the target real or effective user matches the caller effective user or when the caller holds scheduling priority capability in the target user namespace.

Priority setting entry validates the target class, clamps the requested niceness into the allowed range, then applies it to a single process, all threads of a process group, or all visible threads of a user, preserving the first permission or capability error while still attempting remaining targets.
Priority queries and updates hold RCU across target lookup, take the task list read lock while walking a process group, and acquire and release a reference when operating on another user identifier.

Per target priority update checks caller permission, requires extra capability to lower niceness, consults the security hook, converts an initial not found placeholder into success once a target is touched, and then applies the new value.
Priority query entry validates the target class and returns the largest converted niceness among matching processes, process group members, or user owned threads, or not found when nothing matches.
User identity lookup hashes by numeric identifier, walks the bucket chain comparing identities, and holds a reference on a match; absence yields no object.
User hash lookup holds the identifier hash spin lock with interrupts saved across the bucket search.
Priority operations return invalid argument for an unknown target class and not found when no process, group member, or user process matches, including when the named user identity has no entry.
